newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche Telekom shares soar to new record.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche Telekom shares soar to new record.

text.p: Shares in German telecommunications giant Deutsche Telekom AG continued their recent rise to hit a record on Friday, just days ahead of the company's annual news conference and a key deadline for domestic shareholders.

After hitting a low of 29 marks ($17.01) in mid-January, Telekom shares have come charging back and on Friday posted an intraday record of 40 marks, or a gain of some 40 percent on the offering price of 28.50 marks on November 18, 1996. Telekom shares closed bourse trade at 39.95, up 3.2 percent.

Industry analysts said the shares were benefiting from the strength of the broader market, saying there was room for more gains and they expected no surprises that could influence investors at the company's results news conference on Tuesday.

The main figures for 1996 have already been announced. At its annual results news conference on May 13 at 0800 GMT, Telekom will release a detailed 1996 balance sheet. It is not expected to give figures for the first quarter of 1997.

Group sales totalled 63.1 billion marks in 1996, up six percent, while income on ordinary activities rose around 50 percent to six billion marks. Industry analysts said they were interested in more details on net earnings and Telekom's costs.
Earnings per share are expected to nearly double in 1997 to two marks or a little higher from just over one mark in 1996 as revenues rise to 70 billion marks, analysts told Reuters.

"Initially, Telekom (shares) suffered because people didn't know what to make of it," said James Riddiough of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, the investment arm of Deutsche Bank, which has an "overweight" recommendation on the shares.

Telekom is making progress cutting debt and reducing staff. Investors are also less worried about regulatory threats as the market opens to competition in January. The German government, which still owns nearly three-fourths of the company, so far has not been tough on Telekom.
As a result, investors were taking a more cautious look at the stock of Telekom's main domestic competitors Mannesmann AG and Veba AG, analysts said.
"We see Telekom shares going up further," said Riddiough. "That implies that we're saying the shares will outperform the DAX by nine percent over the next nine months."

One surprise that could fuel interest in Telekom would be successful conclusion of talks about a partnership between the Global One alliance of Telekom, France Telecom and Sprint Corp with Cable and Wireless.

Telekom declines to comment on issue, but such an alliance is widely expected. It would be seen as positive for Telekom after a recent round of successes by the rival Concert alliance of British Telecom and MCI

Oliver Ehrenberg, telecoms analyst at Robert Fleming Securities in London, said he has Telekom on a "hold" rating and expects the company to perform "like any other German blue-chip" in line with the market with few surprises.
"I'm going for 16 percent earnings growth from now until the year 2000," he said. "Most major institutions are aware of this so I don't think there will be any major buying."
"Telekom has been a neutral performer. I don't think it will be an outperformer, but it shouldn't underperform," he said. "Telekom is one of our favoured plays in the sector."
An additional boost could come from Germany's planned tax reform. Bonn plans to scrap some corporate taxes next year and Telekom could reap huge savings.

"The tax reform will lead to improved net earnings. Just scrapping taxes on assets and trading capital alone should make savings of 1.2 billion marks possible," said BHF Bank analyst Juergen Elfers in a recent note on the company.

This could boost net per share profit 85 pfennigs from 1999. The effect could be larger in its balance sheet according to U.S. accounting standards, making the share "more attractive to American investors".
Telekom's domestic investors face a test of faith on May 20. That ends a six-month period during which sales of Telekom shares would have been met with heavy taxes on capital gains.

After May 20, that tax no longer applies, but analysts were confident that potential share price gains and Telekom's pledge of bonus shares for those who retain their stock for three years will keep domestic shareholders on board.
"I don't think anything will happen," said Ehrenberg.
-- Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097 145 ($ = 1.704 German Marks)
